title: Majorization and weak majorization
subtitle: G2 lecture 055000 · expanded companion
adaptation: Standalone slide treatment of the spoken lecture and display-only mathematical appendix; authored derivations, worked calculations and local SVG diagrams.

slides.title: Comparing sorted lists
slides.lead: Majorization compares the distribution of mass across a list rather than asking for componentwise domination.
body: Sort x and y into decreasing nonnegative order and pad with zeros to the same finite length. A weak-majorization comparison asks that every prefix of x has no more mass than the corresponding prefix of y.
This is exactly the language naturally produced by Ky Fan inequalities for singular values. It lets two lists be compared even when some individual coordinates move in opposite directions.
slides.takeaway: Weak majorization is a family of sorted partial-sum inequalities.

slides.title: Ordinary majorization also preserves the total
slides.lead: Adding equality of the full totals strengthens weak majorization to majorization.
body: The example x=(3,3,0) and y=(5,1,0) satisfies prefix comparisons 3≤5, 6=6, and 6=6. Thus x is majorized by y. It is a more balanced allocation of the same mass.
If the totals differ, ordinary majorization does not apply even if every prefix comparison holds. The weaker relation is still meaningful and is the one needed for many norm inequalities.
slides.takeaway: Equal total mass distinguishes ordinary from weak majorization.
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 055000 · Ordinary majorization also preserves the total

slides.title: Every prefix is needed
slides.lead: An inequality on the total sum alone cannot determine which list is more concentrated.
body: For x=(4,1,1) and y=(3,3,0), both totals are six, but x has a larger first prefix (4>3), while y has a larger second prefix (6>5). Neither list majorizes the other.
This example illustrates why the definition requires all k, not only k=1 or k=n: intermediate prefixes carry independent information.
slides.takeaway: Equal totals do not imply comparable sorted lists.

slides.title: Summation by parts converts prefixes into weights
slides.lead: Suppose the weights a₁≥···≥aₙ≥0 are decreasing.
body: Write each coordinate as a difference of consecutive prefix sums. Collecting terms rewrites the weighted difference between y and x as nonnegative differences of their prefix sums multiplied by nonnegative differences of the weights.
If x is weakly majorized by y, every term in this expansion is nonnegative. This proves weighted domination without requiring coordinatewise comparison.
slides.takeaway: Decreasing nonnegative weights preserve weak-majorization order.
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 055000 · Summation by parts converts prefixes into weights

slides.title: A weighted numerical example
body: The x-weighted sum equals 4·3+2·3=18; the y-weighted sum equals 4·5+2·1=22. Their difference is four.
The prefix gaps are (2,0,0). The weight differences are (2,1) and the final weight is 1; the summation-by-parts formula gives 2·2+1·0+1·0=4, matching the direct computation.
slides.takeaway: The numerical calculation exposes the exact role of the first prefix gap.

slides.title: A transfer evens out two coordinates
slides.lead: Moving some mass from a larger coordinate to a smaller one preserves the total but makes the list less concentrated.
body: Starting from (5,1), moving two units from the first entry to the second gives (3,3). Algebraically this is averaging a vector with its coordinate-swapped copy.
Such two-coordinate transfers generate ordinary majorization in finite dimensions. They also provide a constructive route to the convexity comparison in the next lecture.
slides.takeaway: Pairwise averaging is the geometric mechanism behind ordinary majorization.
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 055000 · A transfer evens out two coordinates

slides.title: Singular values translate matrix inequalities into list inequalities
slides.lead: For any matrix A, the k largest singular values form the kth Ky Fan sum.
body: Therefore Kₖ(A)≤Kₖ(B) for every k is exactly the statement σ(A)≺_w σ(B), after matching lengths by zeros. This is a powerful compression of infinitely many potential norm arguments into one list comparison.
We can use it for pinching, triangular estimates, and comparisons between operator measurements without checking each gauge separately.
slides.takeaway: Ky Fan domination and weak majorization are the same data in two notations.
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 055000 · Singular values translate matrix inequalities into list inequalities

slides.title: Limits of the definition
slides.lead: Sorting and common length are essential parts of the comparison.
body: A list written in an arbitrary coordinate order can have prefix sums that change under relabeling; those are not the invariants majorization studies. Negative coordinates also require a more careful general definition than the nonnegative singular-value version used here.

When working with rectangular matrices, pad the shorter singular-value list by zeros and sort both lists before comparing. That makes the statement independent of matrix coordinates and shape conventions.
slides.takeaway: Sort, pad with zeros, and specify whether the totals must agree.

slides.title: Weak and ordinary majorization play different roles
slides.lead: Concentration comparisons usually preserve total mass; norm domination often does not.
body: Ordinary majorization supports the picture of repeated two-coordinate transfers because those preserve sums. Weak majorization also allows reductions in total mass, so its constructive description requires coordinatewise shrinking as well.
That extra step explains why sign invariance joins convexity and permutation symmetry in the norm-dominance theorem that follows.
slides.takeaway: Weak majorization adds the possibility of loss of total mass.
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 055000 · Weak and ordinary majorization play different roles

slides.title: Reconstruct the comparison
slides.lead: Start from two decreasing nonnegative lists and compare each prefix.
body: Then derive the weighted summation-by-parts identity using telescoping sums. Check it on x=(3,3,0), y=(5,1,0), with weights (4,2,1).
Finally, translate a Ky Fan inequality for matrices into a weak-majorization statement about their singular values. The complete argument uses only sorted prefixes and elementary sums.
slides.takeaway: Prefix inequalities are the reusable unit of spectral norm comparison.
